entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13043"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Zech.3.1-Zech.3.10">Zec 3:1-10</reference>. Fourth Vision. Joshua the high priest before the angel of Jehovah; accused by Satan, but justified by Jehovah through Messiah the coming Branch.</title> <div sID="gen24489" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13043"/>1. Joshua as high priest (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.1">Hag 1:1</reference>) represents "Jerusalem" (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.2">Zec 3:2</reference>), or the elect people, put on its trial, and "plucked" narrowly "out of the fire." His attitude, "standing before the Lord," is that of a high priest ministering before the altar erected previously to the building of the temple (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.2">Ezr 3:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.6">3, 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.135.2">Psa 135:2</reference>). Yet, in this position, by reason of his own and his people's sins, he is represented as on his and their trial (<reference osisRef="Num.35.12">Nu 35:12</reference>).<div eID="gen24489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24490" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he showed me--</hi>"He" is the interpreting angel. Jerusalem's (Joshua's) "filthy garments" (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.3">Zec 3:3</reference>) are its sins which had hitherto brought down God's judgments. The "change of raiment" implies its restoration to God's favor. Satan suggested to the Jews that so consciously polluted a priesthood and people could offer no acceptable sacrifice to God, and therefore they might as well desist from the building of the temple. Zechariah encourages them by showing that their demerit does not disqualify them for the work, as they are accepted in the righteousness of another, their great High Priest, the Branch (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.8">Zec 3:8</reference>), a scion of their own royal line of David (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Is 11:1</reference>). The full accomplishment of Israel's justification and of Satan the accuser's being "rebuked" finally, is yet future (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.10">Re 12:10</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Rev.11.8">Re 11:8</reference>, wherein "Jerusalem," as here, is shown to be meant primarily, though including the whole Church in general (compare <reference osisRef="Job.1.9">Job 1:9</reference>).<div eID="gen24490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24491" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Satan--</hi>the Hebrew term meaning "adversary" in a law court: as devil is the Greek term, meaning accuser. Messiah, on the other hand, is "advocate" for His people in the court of heaven's justice (<reference osisRef="1John.2.1">1Jo 2:1</reference>).<div eID="gen24491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24492" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">standing at his right hand--</hi>the usual position of a prosecutor or accuser in court, as the left hand was the position of the defendant (<reference osisRef="Ps.109.6">Psa 109:6</reference>). The "angel of the Lord" took the same position just before another high priest was about to beget the forerunner of Messiah (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.11">Lu 1:11</reference>), who supplants Satan from his place as accuser. Some hence explain Jude 9 as referring to this passage: "the body of Moses" being thus the Jewish Church, for which Satan contended as his by reason of its sins; just as the "body of Christ" is the Christian Church. However, Jude 9 plainly speaks of the literal body of Moses, the resurrection of which at the transfiguration Satan seems to have opposed on the ground of Moses' error at Meribah; the same divine rebuke, "the Lord rebuke thee," checked Satan in contending for judgment against Moses' body, as checked him when demanding judgment against the Jewish Church, to which Moses' body corresponds. <div eID="gen24492" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 3 Zec 3:1-10 . Fourth Vision. Joshua the high priest before the angel of Jehovah; accused by Satan, but justified by Jehovah through Messiah the coming Branch. 1. Joshua as high priest ( Hag 1:1 ) represents "Jerusalem" ( Zec 3:2 ), or the elect people, put on its trial, and "plucked" narrowly "out of the fire." His attitude, "standing before the Lord," is that of a high priest ministering before the altar erected previously to the building of the temple ( Ezr 3:2 , 3, 6 ; Psa 135:2 ). Yet, in this position, by reason of his own and his people's sins, he is represented as on his and their trial ( Nu 35:12 ). he showed me-- "He" is the interpreting angel. Jerusalem's (Joshua's) "filthy garments" ( Zec 3:3 ) are its sins which had hitherto brought down God's judgments. The "change of raiment" implies its restoration to God's favor. Satan suggested to the Jews that so consciously polluted a priesthood and people could offer no acceptable sacrifice to God, and therefore they might as well desist from the building of the temple. Zechariah encourages them by showing that their demerit does not disqualify them for the work, as they are accepted in the righteousness of another, their great High Priest, the Branch ( Zec 3:8 ), a scion of their own royal line of David ( Is 11:1 ). The full accomplishment of Israel's justification and of Satan the accuser's being "rebuked" finally, is yet future ( Re 12:10 ). Compare Re 11:8 , wherein "Jerusalem," as here, is shown to be meant primarily, though including the whole Church in general (compare Job 1:9 ). Satan-- the Hebrew term meaning "adversary" in a law court: as devil is the Greek term, meaning accuser. Messiah, on the other hand, is "advocate" for His people in the court of heaven's justice ( 1Jo 2:1 ). standing at his right hand-- the usual position of a prosecutor or accuser in court, as the left hand was the position of the defendant ( Psa 109:6 ). The "angel of the Lord" took the same position just before another high priest was about to beget the forerunner of Messiah ( Lu 1:11 ), who supplants Satan from his place as accuser. Some hence explain Jude 9 as referring to this passage: "the body of Moses" being thus the Jewish Church, for which Satan contended as his by reason of its sins; just as the "body of Christ" is the Christian Church. However, Jude 9 plainly speaks of the literal body of Moses, the resurrection of which at the transfiguration Satan seems to have opposed on the ground of Moses' error at Meribah; the same divine rebuke, "the Lord rebuke thee," checked Satan in contending for judgment against Moses' body, as checked him when demanding judgment against the Jewish Church, to which Moses' body corresponds.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13044"/><div sID="gen24493" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13044"/><hi type="bold">2. the Lord--</hi>Jehovah, hereby identified with the "angel of the Lord (Jehovah)" (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.1">Zec 3:1</reference>).<div eID="gen24493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24494" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rebuke thee--</hi>twice repeated to express the certainty of Satan's accusations and machinations against Jerusalem being frustrated. Instead of lengthened argument, Jehovah silences Satan by the one plea, namely, God's choice.<div eID="gen24494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24495" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chosen Jerusalem--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rom.9.16">Ro 9:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.5">11:5</reference>). The conclusive answer. If the issue rested on Jerusalem's merit or demerit, condemnation must be the award; but Jehovah's "choice" (<reference osisRef="John.15.16">Joh 15:16</reference>) rebuts Satan's charge against Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.17">Zec 1:17</reference>; 2:12; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.33">Ro 8:33</reference>, 34, 37), represented by Joshua (compare in the great atonement, <reference osisRef="Lev.16.6-Lev.16.20">Le 16:6-20</reference>, &c.), not that she may continue in sin, but be freed from it (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.7">Zec 3:7</reference>).<div eID="gen24495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24496" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brand plucked out of ... fire--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Amos.4.11">Am 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.18">1Pe 4:18</reference>; Jude 23). Herein God implies that His acquittal of Jerusalem is not that He does not recognize her sin (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.3">Zec 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.4.9">4, 9</reference>), but that having punished her people for it with a seventy years' captivity, He on the ground of His electing love has delivered her from the fiery ordeal; and when once He has begun a deliverance, as in this case, He will perfect it (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.30-Ps.89.35">Psa 89:30-35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.6">Php 1:6</reference>). <div eID="gen24496" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13045"/><div sID="gen24497" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13045"/><hi type="bold">3. filthy garments--</hi>symbol of sin (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.12">Pr 30:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.4.4">Is 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.64.6">64:6</reference>); proving that it is not on the ground of His people's righteousness that He accepts them. Here primarily the "filthy garments" represent the abject state temporally of the priesthood and people at the return from Babylon. Yet he "stood before the angel." Abject as he was, he was before Jehovah's eye, who graciously accepts His people's services, though mixed with sin and infirmity. <div eID="gen24497" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13046"/><div sID="gen24498" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13046"/><hi type="bold">4. those that stood before him--</hi>the ministering angels (compare the phrase in <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.8">1Ki 10:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.1.5">Da 1:5</reference>).<div eID="gen24498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24499" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Take away the filthy garments--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Zech.3.9">Zec 3:9</reference> it is "remove the iniquity of that land"; therefore Joshua represents the land.<div eID="gen24499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24500" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from him--</hi>literally, "from upon him"; pressing upon him as an overwhelming burden.<div eID="gen24500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24501" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">change of raiment--</hi>festal robes of the high priest, most costly and gorgeous; symbol of Messiah's imputed righteousness (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.11">Mt 22:11</reference>). The restoration of the glory of the priesthood is implied: first, partially, at the completion of the second temple; fully realized in the great High Priest Jesus, whose name is identical with Joshua (<reference osisRef="Heb.4.8">He 4:8</reference>), the Representative of Israel, the "kingdom of priests" (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">Ex 19:6</reference>); once clad in the filthy garments of our vileness, but being the chosen of the Father (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Is 42:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.1">44:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.1-Isa.49.3">49:1-3</reference>), He hath by death ceased from sin, and in garments of glory entered the heavenly holy place as our High Priest (<reference osisRef="Heb.8.1">He 8:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.24">9:24</reference>). Then, as the consequence (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.5">1Pe 2:5</reference>), realized in the Church generally (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.22">Lu 15:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.8">Re 19:8</reference>), and in Israel in particular (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.10">Is 61:10</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.3.6">Is 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.21">66:21</reference>). <div eID="gen24501" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 4. those that stood before him-- the ministering angels (compare the phrase in 1Ki 10:8 ; Da 1:5 ). Take away the filthy garments-- In Zec 3:9 it is "remove the iniquity of that land"; therefore Joshua represents the land. from him-- literally, "from upon him"; pressing upon him as an overwhelming burden. change of raiment-- festal robes of the high priest, most costly and gorgeous; symbol of Messiah's imputed righteousness ( Mt 22:11 ). The restoration of the glory of the priesthood is implied: first, partially, at the completion of the second temple; fully realized in the great High Priest Jesus, whose name is identical with Joshua ( He 4:8 ), the Representative of Israel, the "kingdom of priests" ( Ex 19:6 ); once clad in the filthy garments of our vileness, but being the chosen of the Father ( Is 42:1 ; 44:1 ; 49:1-3 ), He hath by death ceased from sin, and in garments of glory entered the heavenly holy place as our High Priest ( He 8:1 ; 9:24 ). Then, as the consequence ( 1Pe 2:5 ), realized in the Church generally ( Lu 15:22 ; Re 19:8 ), and in Israel in particular ( Is 61:10 ; compare Is 3:6 ; 66:21 ).

Hear--</hi>On account of the magnitude of what He is about to say, He at once demands solemn attention.<div eID="gen24510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24511" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy fellows that sit before thee--</hi>thy subordinate colleagues in the priesthood; not that they were actually then sitting before him; but their usual posture in consultations was on chairs or benches before him, while he sat on an elevated seat as their president.<div eID="gen24511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24512" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they are--</hi>From speaking to Joshua He passes to speaking of him and them, in the third person, to the attendant angels (compare <reference osisRef="Zech.3.9">Zec 3:9</reference>).<div eID="gen24512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24513" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">men wondered at--</hi>Hebrew, "men of wonder," that is, having a typical character (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.18">Is 8:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.20.3">20:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.11">Eze 12:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.24">24:24</reference>). The reference cannot be to Zerubbabel (as Grotius thinks), for he was then in the full discharge of his office, whereas "the Branch" here is regarded as future. <div eID="gen24516" type="x-p"/>

Joshua the high priest typifies Messiah, as Joshua's "fellows" typify believers whom Messiah admits to share His Priesthood ( 1Pe 2:5 ; Re 5:10 ). This, its typical character, then, is a pledge to assure the desponding Jews that the priesthood shall be preserved till the great Antitype comes. There may be also an indirect reproof of the unbelief of the multitude who "wonder" at God's servants and even at God's Son incredulously ( Psa 71:7 ; Is 8:18 ; 53:1 , &c.). behold-- marking the greatness of what follows. my servant-- the characteristic title of Messiah ( Is 42:1 ; 49:3 ; 50:10 ; 52:13 ; 53:11 ; Eze 34:23 , 24 ). the Branch-- Messiah, a tender branch from the almost extinct royal line of David ( Zec 6:12 ; Is 4:2 ; 11:1 ; Jr 23:5 ; 33:15 ). Lu 1:78 , where for "day spring," "branch" may be substituted (Mal 4:2, however, favors English Version). The reference cannot be to Zerubbabel (as Grotius thinks), for he was then in the full discharge of his office, whereas "the Branch" here is regarded as future.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13051"/><div sID="gen24517" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13051"/><hi type="bold">9. For--</hi>expressing the ground for encouragement to the Jews in building the temple: I (Jehovah) have laid the (foundation) stone as the chief architect, before (in the presence of) Joshua, by "the hand of Zerubbabel" (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.10">Zec 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.8-Ezra.3.13">Ezr 3:8-13</reference>), so that your labor in building shall not be vain. Antitypically, the (foundation) stone alluded to is Christ, before called "the Branch." Lest any should think from that term that His kingdom is weak, He now calls it "the stone," because of its solidity and strength whereby it is to be the foundation of the Church, and shall crush all the world kingdoms (<reference osisRef="Ps.118.22">Psa 118:22</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Is 28:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.2.45">Da 2:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.21.42">Mt 21:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.11">1Co 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.6">1Pe 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.7">7</reference>). The angel pointing to the chief stone lying before Him, intimates that a deeper mystery than the material temple is symbolized. Moore thinks the "stone" is the Jewish Church, which Jehovah engages watchfully to guard. The temple, rather, is that symbolically. But the antitype of the foundation-stone is Messiah.<div eID="gen24517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24518" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon one stone shall be seven eyes--</hi>namely, the watchful "eyes" of Jehovah's care ever fixed "upon" it (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.10">Zec 4:10</reference>) [Maurer]. The eye is the symbol of Providence: "seven," of perfection (<reference osisRef="Rev.5.6">Re 5:6</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9">2Ch 16:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.32.8">Psa 32:8</reference>). Antitypically, "the seven eyes upon the stone" are the eyes of all angels (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference>), and of all saints (<reference osisRef="John.3.14">Joh 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.3.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.32">12:32</reference>), and of the patriarchs and prophets (<reference osisRef="John.8.56">Joh 8:56</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.10">1Pe 1:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.11">11</reference>), fixed on Christ; above all, the eyes of the Father ever rest with delight on Him. Calvin (perhaps better) considers the seven eyes to be carved on the stone, that is, not the eyes of the Father and of angels and saints ever fixed on Him, but His own sevenfold (perfect) fullness of grace, and of gifts of the Spirit (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.2">Is 11:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.16">Joh 1:16</reference>; 3:34; <reference osisRef="Col.1.19">Col 1:19</reference>; 2:9), and His watchful providence now for the Jews in building the temple, and always for His Church, His spiritual temple. Thus the "stone" is not as other stones senseless, but living and full of eyes of perfect intelligence (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.4">1Pe 2:4</reference>, "a living stone"), who not only attracts the eyes (<reference osisRef="John.12.32">Joh 12:32</reference>) of His people, but emits illumination so as to direct them to Him.<div eID="gen24518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24519" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">engrave ... graving--</hi>implying Messiah's exceeding beauty and preciousness; alluding to the polished stones of the temple: Christ excelled them, as much as God who "prepared His body" (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.5">He 10:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="John.2.21">Joh 2:21</reference>) is superior to all human builders.<div eID="gen24519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24520" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remove ... iniquity of that land in one day--</hi>that is, the iniquity and its consequences, namely the punishment to which the Jews heretofore had been subjected (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.6">Hag 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9-1Cor.1.11">9-11</reference>). The remission of sin is the fountain of every other blessing. The "one day" of its removal is primarily the day of national atonement celebrated after the completion of the temple (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.27">Le 23:27</reference>) on the tenth day of the seventh month. Antitypically, the atonement by Messiah for all men, once for all ("one day") offered, needing no repetition like the Mosaic sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.10">He 10:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.14">12, 14</reference>). <div eID="gen24520" type="x-p"/>
